doc.title: Tony Parenti and Anthony Sbarbaro Interview, 1959-06-29

title: Edwards runs the Original Dixieland Band; later Barry, Detroit and gumbo
summary: Edwards, not LaRocca, leading the band, Fritzl raises, later musicians in California, and talk of gumbo.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well, Merritt and Henry. No, no. Well, Merritt was a trumpet player. There's only two trombone players. George and... George came, you know, later. But Henry was the... There was two trombones that Ernest Giordina used. And that was Eddie Edwards and Henry Brunas. They were two of the kings down there. It was... You might have heard about Tom Brown, but they could never play with Giordina's band, because Giordina would play stuff out unorthodox. You understand? He played more. Brown would only play what he knew, and he would play it good. But he could never sit in a situation with Edwards, no more than I could sit in a ring right now with Gene Krupa. It's actually, you've got to speak up truth, you know? But when they got up to Chicago, immediately they started fighting, which is nothing new. And remember this. I told you that they gave me an increase in this black cap where I was working, because that was the number two cabaret on the street. I got the big sum of two dollars a night. I was getting fourteen dollars a week, you know, from 10.50. I got a half a dollar raise, and I didn't want to leave. So they were only making 25 dollars a week in Chicago. It didn't pay me to go to Chicago. So Edwards got me, kept around, and finally I decided, well, I'll give it a try. And I went up there. But Yellow Nunes was still in the band. They had gotten rid of Stein. Now they're going to reorganize the band, and that's when they call it the Original Dixieland Band. And who was the leader then? No, Eddie Edwards was the leader. He really ran everything. Eddie Edwards was running a band. Not Nick LaRocca. Not Nick LaRocca. Eddie Edwards was running that band, because, listen, the difference in musicianship and the difference between any way, shape, or form, there was one man in the band that knew music, and that was Eddie Edwards. Yeah, he was, and also he was the business value of the band, too. But then again, after that, they start fighting, Yellow started getting so funny, they lined up shields, and they put shields in the band. Then they call it the Original Dixieland Jazz Band. And that was it. That was, uh... Well, you know, the reason why I brought this up, because right after that happened, Johnny Stein came to New Orleans. Look up men. Look up men. He came over to my house. That's right. And you know, I've been all confused, and that's why I'm asking you. You see, I thought it was Eddie Edwards that came to my house, but I think it was Johnny Stein who came and asked me and my mother. I'll tell you why that could be, because there were jobs for jazz bands in Chicago, and Johnny Stein was already there, and he figures, why should I go back to New Orleans, get a man, and go back there again? Get another band. Which he did go back with some other fellas who I don't know of. Because I was still in my short bands. But I distinctly remember, we got 25 hours a week, and I was working four days with the band when they... we had a fight with the boss. I think we won the 35 or something, and he fired us. And I'm out of work, with only four days pay in my pocket. And then we went to work in another place for Reeves. And then he gave us, kept giving us increases. And a man by the name of who owns the Chapery in Chicago right now, Mike Fritzl, owns the Chapery still. He would always offer us ten dollars a week more than what we were getting. He was the one that spiked the band on to get raises. So first thing you know, we got a raise, and then we come back to the boss. We didn't want to leave this place we were working, because Harry James, they were nice to us. But Mike Fritzl kept talking to us. Then, by that time, New York came through, and that was a big sum of something like 75 hours a week. That's a lot. Oh, by that time we were rich, you know, we thought we were rich men. So from then on, everybody. But at the very beginning there, you know, it was never called the original Dixieland Jazz. It was Stein's band from Dixieland. You know? And it wasn't that, as I say, fights can happen. They're happening right now. Look how many bands split up right now, you know? And you know something, Tony? That was the end of me seeing you for many years, because when I saw you. Well, I used to go to New Orleans when you were working in this theater, but I never used to, because you fellas, if you remember, you were doing about at least three a day. Oh yeah, I know. And I could never, your show, and I could never, for some reason I never got back there. And I always wondered, I used to know the name of some of the fellas in the band, and it skipped me. Wasn't Santa Picora on trombone, or? Well, no, wait a while. Or was it Barry? No, wait a while. Barry. Melville. We, don't forget, Melville Barry used to play with us when Johnny Detrott and I, and Paul Detrott and Tom Zimmerman, he died years ago, when we had the band at the Roosevelt, now the Groove, I mean it was the Grooveall band. Yeah. It was the Forest Club or something, that Forest, something, Forest something, on Barone Street side, Hendricks. And we had the band there. And then Melville Barry left in Santa Picora, and he was Barry on trombone. Yeah, he left, he went to California. Well, I met him, I met him in Detroit, out in California, when we were out there during the war. That was in, uh, well, World War year, whatever it was, in the 40s. You know, early 40s. Oh yeah. We were out there with Catherine Dunn, and Brad Brown was with us. Oh, that's the Second World War. Yeah, Second World War. Yeah. Well, Barry and Detroit were one of the two boys that were in on the ground floor of that, uh, music out there. You know, they got in on the ground floor, and they was telling us all about that, because both of them were excellent, excellent musicians. They must have been the same. Yes, they were. Uh, Barry was a nice little musician. He could read. Paul DePort was a very fine drummer, and he could read. So when he got out to California, they did a lot of stuff, and studio work, and many other things, incidentally. He's been out there all these years. Yeah. And he's done very fine. They were the first ones. That's right. Getting on that ground floor. But, uh, but I used to come in the theater where you were working, because I never knew Tony before you. I never saw you. No, well, that's just it. Because the way you look now, boy, and the way you look there. Oh yeah, I was as skinny as a red. You were skinny as a rail, and you had all kinds of funny looking, uh, things around your face there. But, uh, not pimples. Tony was the cutest little character in the world, but there he is now, healthy looking. How much you weigh now? Oh, about 185. You know how much you were weighing then? You weren't weighing no more than 90 pounds. I was always skinny, yeah. Well, you know why I weigh a lot now? I drink all that beer down to Nick's down there, down to the Metropole, some of those places. Well, no, you still go for that little New Orleans cooking Glutzen Adelie. You know I'm cooking back there in the kitchen. Oh, boy. You know what I'm cooking, aren't you? And I'll never lose the love for that old basic Creole dish, so to speak. Gumbo. Gumbo. I want to tell you something. I still say I make trips to New Orleans, and it's getting bad in some of those places down there where they skip it up on those famous dishes. I went to several places down there, and I see this gumbo on the bill of fare, and that's gumbo for me. Well, brother, when I get it served, it don't taste like the gumbo I used to eat. What kind of gumbo is it? I don't know what it is, but I'm making gumbo with the okra. I still have a taste in my mouth for decent food, thank God, but some of those restaurants down there, they'll lead you to them. You got to keep your mouth shut because they may say... Oh, they give you that watery stuff. I don't know what they give me, Tony. There's all kinds of ways of making gumbo. You can make it with chicken and crabs and... I don't want to mention the name of some of those places, and there's not no, you know, no water or shit. Well, you got those famous places there. They can't give you nothing but the right way. I mean, like, I don't know, Antoine's and La Louisiana's are not anymore. That's, uh, that boy... But you see what, I see what happens. This is our natural, we have people that come up here, and when they come up here, yeah, they visit my kids and all, and we put them up, you know, and that's when I go down there, they want to reciprocate, you understand? They want to show me good, and they'll take me to some of the fine spots. Food is not like it used to be, and there's still plenty of good places down there. That's, that's for, that's for sure. We ought to start talking about some of those, uh, early bands around there, the Jack Lane stuff, because he is the, Jack Lane is the, really the historian, you know. He can sure play, he can
